content: Digestion is the biological process by which the gastrointestinal (GI) tract breaks down food into smaller components to enable absorption of nutrients essential for health and energy. This process involves several organs including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and accessory organs such as the pancreas, liver, and gallbladder. Digestion begins with mechanical breakdown, such as chewing, and continues with chemical breakdown through enzymes and acids. Major mechanisms include enzymatic hydrolysis of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats to their absorbable units like glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids. The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption, aided by villi and microvilli that increase surface area. Practical relevance of understanding digestion includes managing nutrition, supporting metabolic health, and addressing digestive disorders. Limitations in current understanding relate to interindividual variability and complex interactions with gut microbiota that influence digestion and health. Important concepts related to digestion include enzyme function, gut motility, pH regulation, and immune protection of the GI lining. Knowing how digestion works helps individuals make informed dietary choices and recognize when to seek medical advice for digestive symptoms.

content: Digestion is a complex process that transforms the foods we eat into nutrients that the body can absorb and use. It involves coordinated actions of the mouth, stomach, intestines, and accessory organs. This section introduces these components and outlines the digestion journey from ingestion to elimination.

content: Mechanical digestion involves physical processes such as chewing in the mouth and muscular contractions in the stomach that physically break food into smaller pieces. These actions increase the surface area available for chemical digestion.

chunk_title: Chemical Digestion: Role of Enzymes and Acids
content: Chemical digestion breaks down complex molecules into simpler ones using enzymes and acids. Salivary amylase begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth, gastric acid and pepsin act in the stomach to denature proteins, and pancreatic enzymes continue digestion in the small intestine.

content: The stomach stores food and mixes it with gastric juices, including hydrochloric acid and digestive enzymes. This environment helps denature proteins and activate enzymes necessary for protein digestion. The stomach also controls the gradual release of partially digested food into the small intestine.

chunk_title: Nutrient Absorption in the Small Intestine
content: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine, which has specialized structures called villi and microvilli that greatly increase the surface area. Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals are absorbed through the intestinal lining into the bloodstream or lymphatic system.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes from indigestible food remnants and compacts waste into feces. It also houses beneficial bacteria that ferment some undigested materials, producing vitamins and gases.

chunk_title: Protective Mechanisms of the Digestive Tract
content: The digestive tract protects itself from harsh digestive chemicals and pathogens through mucus secretions, tight junctions between epithelial cells, immune cells, and normal gut flora that inhibit harmful microbes.

chunk_title: Supporting Digestive Health and Common Disorders
content: Lifestyle factors such as diet, hydration, and physical activity influence digestive health. Common conditions affecting digestion include acid reflux, irritable bowel syndrome, and enzyme deficiencies. Awareness and healthy habits can help maintain optimal digestive function.
